547.summary: isConnected is an adjacency matrix describing connections between cities, not a land-and-water grid. Directly or indirectly connected cities form one province.
547.pitfall: Visit city numbers, not matrix cells. If 0 and 1 connect and 2 is isolated, the groups are {0,1} and {2}. Diagonal entries do not create extra provinces.
547.notation: n is the number of cities. The input n × n matrix is excluded from extra space. Both BFS and DFS scan n entries for each of n cities. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

methods.name: BFS with a queue (recommended)
methods.idea: Start a search whenever you find an unvisited city. Each new search discovers one province.
steps: visited stores city numbers. ans counts the provinces found so far.
For an unvisited city i, increase ans, put i in dq, and mark it visited. Repeatedly use popleft() and add connected unvisited cities.
When the queue is empty, this province is complete. Each of n cities scans a row of n entries: O(n²) time. The queue and visited set use O(n) space.

methods.name: DFS with a stack
methods.idea: Use the same structure as BFS, but visit the most recently discovered city first.
steps: Keep the same visited set, answer counter, and outer loop over cities.
Replace deque([i]) with [i], and popleft() with pop(). Mark each city when adding it to the stack.
Each city still scans one complete row: O(n²) time. The stack and visited set use O(n) space, without recursive calls.

methods.name: Union-Find
methods.idea: Begin with n separate groups. Each successful merge reduces the group count by one.
steps: parent starts with each city as its own representative. size tracks group sizes, and ans starts at n.
find follows parent links to the representative and shortens the path. For each connected pair, compare their representatives.
If the representatives differ, attach the smaller group to the larger one and decrease ans. Scan only j > i because the matrix is symmetric. Extra space is O(n).

802.summary: A node is safe only if every possible path from it eventually ends. Exclude cycles and nodes that can reach a cycle.
802.pitfall: Having one route to a terminal node is not enough. Every possible route must terminate.

methods.name: Reverse topological sorting
methods.idea: Start with terminal nodes, then work backward to discover other safe nodes.
steps: Build reverse_graph and count each node's outgoing edges.
Put nodes with no outgoing edges into dq. Removing a safe node reduces its predecessors' remaining outgoing counts.
A predecessor becomes safe when its count reaches zero. Return safe nodes in numerical order.

methods.name: Three-state DFS
methods.idea: A node is safe only if every path from it ends.
steps: Use state 0 for unvisited, 1 for an active or unsafe node, and 2 for a confirmed safe node.
Reaching state 1 means the current route cannot be confirmed safe. Recursively check every neighbor before setting state 2.
Reuse confirmed results. A long chain can exceed Python's recursion limit; prefer the iterative method for large inputs.

methods.name: Check each reachable subgraph
methods.idea: For each starting node, separately check whether its reachable subgraph contains a cycle.
steps: Collect every node reachable from the starting node.
Compute indegrees within that subgraph and remove zero-indegree nodes using a queue.
If all reachable nodes are removed, the starting node is safe. This repeats work and is useful mainly for understanding or small inputs.

802.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

841.summary: Visiting a room gives you its keys. Find all rooms reachable from room 0.
841.pitfall: A key is usable only after you reach the room containing it.

methods.name: DFS with a stack
methods.idea: Follow the keys available from room 0.
steps: Start with visited = {0} and stack = [0].
Pop a room. For each key in that room, add its room to visited and the stack if it is new.
All rooms are reachable exactly when len(visited) equals len(rooms).

methods.name: BFS with a queue
methods.idea: Use a queue to visit rooms as their keys become available.
steps: Start with room 0 in visited and dq.
Use popleft() to take the next room. Add every newly unlocked room to visited before putting it in the queue.
Compare the number of visited rooms with the total number of rooms.

methods.name: Repeated reachable-set expansion
methods.idea: Keep collecting keys until no new room can be unlocked.
steps: Start with only room 0 reachable.
Copy the reachable set and add the keys from every currently reachable room.
If the set stops changing, compare its size with the number of rooms. Repeated scans make this slower than BFS or DFS.

841.notation: V is the number of rooms and K is the total number of keys. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1129.summary: Your next valid move depends on the last edge color. Represent a state as (node, last color).
1129.pitfall: Do not mark only the node as visited. Allow both color states at the starting node.

methods.name: BFS over node-and-color states
methods.idea: Track both the current node and the color of the last edge.
steps: Build separate adjacency lists for red and blue edges. Initialize both color states at node 0 with distance 0.
Pop a state from the queue and follow only edges of the opposite color.
Store the shortest distance for each state. For each node, return the smaller distance, or -1 if neither state is reachable.

methods.name: Dijkstra over node-and-color states
methods.idea: Use a heap to process the state with the shortest distance first.
steps: Store distances separately for the two possible last-edge colors.
Pop a state, ignore outdated entries, and try edges of the opposite color.
Push improved states into the heap. This works, but BFS is simpler because every edge costs one step.

methods.name: Repeated relaxation
methods.idea: Repeatedly improve distances until no improvement remains.
steps: Keep two distances per node, one for each last-edge color.
Scan all transitions. A transition must change color and adds one to the distance.
Repeat up to 2V rounds, stopping early if nothing changes. Take the minimum of the two distances at each node.

1129.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1376.summary: Direct reports receive the news in parallel. The answer is the latest arrival time among all employees.
1376.pitfall: Do not sum independent branches. A leaf has informTime 0, and headID need not be 0.

methods.name: Tree DFS
methods.idea: Track when each employee receives the news, using a stack.
steps: Build the list of direct reports from manager.
Start at headID with time 0. For each report, add the current manager's informTime to the arrival time.
Keep the maximum arrival time. Reports receive the news in parallel, so do not add the times of separate branches.

methods.name: Tree BFS
methods.idea: Use a queue to propagate arrival times down the management tree.
steps: Build the list of direct reports and enqueue (headID, 0).
Pop an employee and update the maximum arrival time.
Enqueue each direct report with the employee's arrival time plus their informTime. Return the maximum.

methods.name: Memoized parent paths
methods.idea: Compute each employee's arrival time by following their manager chain.
steps: Record arrival[headID] = 0.
For each employee, follow managers until reaching an employee whose arrival time is known. Save the unknown chain.
Walk back down the saved chain, adding each manager's informTime. Return the largest recorded arrival time.

1376.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1466.summary: The undirected structure is a tree. When rooted at city 0, every road must point toward its parent.
1466.pitfall: An input edge [u,v] means u → v. During outward traversal from 0, edges matching the traversal direction need reversing.

methods.name: DFS with direction costs
methods.idea: Explore outward from city 0 and count edges that point the wrong way.
steps: For each original edge u → v, store (v, 1) at u and (u, 0) at v.
Start a stack at city 0. Visit each new city once.
Add the stored cost when crossing to a new city. A cost of 1 means the original edge must be reversed.

methods.name: BFS with direction costs
methods.idea: Use the same direction costs, but explore with a queue.
steps: Build adjacency entries in both directions, with reversal costs 1 and 0.
Start dq and visited with city 0.
Pop a city, add each new neighbor's reversal cost, mark it visited, and enqueue it.

methods.name: Root the tree first
methods.idea: Find each city's parent toward city 0, then compare the original directions.
steps: Treat all roads as undirected and build a parent array rooted at 0.
Traverse the tree to assign each city's parent.
An original edge u → v needs reversing exactly when parent[v] == u, because it points away from the root.

1466.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1192.summary: Find bridges: edges whose removal disconnects the graph. A DFS child needs its parent edge when it cannot reach an earlier ancestor another way.
1192.pitfall: The bridge condition is low[child] > discovery[parent], not >=. Prefer iterative DFS for large graphs.

methods.name: Iterative Tarjan
methods.idea: Use discovery times and the earliest reachable ancestor to find bridges without recursion.
steps: Build an undirected graph. Record discovery and low values when first visiting a node.
Keep a stack of nodes and neighbor iterators. When a child finishes, propagate its low value to its parent.
If the child's low value is greater than the parent's discovery time, their connecting edge is a bridge.

methods.name: Recursive Tarjan
methods.idea: A DFS child needs its parent edge if it cannot reach an earlier ancestor another way.
steps: Give each newly visited node a discovery time and initialize its low value.
Recurse into unvisited neighbors. For already visited non-parent neighbors, lower the current low value using their discovery time.
After returning from a child, test low[child] > discovery[parent]. Long paths may exceed Python's recursion limit.

methods.name: Remove each edge and rebuild groups
methods.idea: An edge is critical if deleting it disconnects the graph.
steps: Choose one edge to skip and start a fresh Union-Find structure.
Merge the endpoints of every other edge.
If more than one connected group remains, record the skipped edge. This is much slower but makes the definition explicit.

1192.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1926.summary: Every move costs one step, so BFS finds a nearest exit. The entrance itself never counts as an exit.
1926.pitfall: Check walls and bounds, and explicitly exclude the entrance from the exit test even when it lies on the boundary.

methods.name: BFS from the entrance
methods.idea: Every move costs one step, so BFS reaches the nearest exit first.
steps: Start at the entrance with distance 0 and mark it visited.
Pop a cell and check whether it is a boundary cell other than the entrance.
Add valid unvisited empty neighbors with distance + 1. Return -1 if no exit is reached.

methods.name: BFS from all exits
methods.idea: Search backward from every valid exit at once.
steps: Collect all empty boundary cells, excluding the entrance itself.
Put all exits in the queue at distance 0 and expand through empty cells.
The first time the entrance is reached gives its shortest distance to an exit.

methods.name: Dijkstra
methods.idea: Use a heap to visit cells in increasing distance order.
steps: Start a heap at the entrance with distance 0.
Pop the nearest cell and check for a valid exit.
Push valid unvisited empty neighbors with distance + 1. Since all moves have equal cost, BFS avoids unnecessary heap work.

1926.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

934.summary: Expand from the entire first island to find the fewest water cells needed to reach the second island.
934.pitfall: There are no additional obstacles in the water. For two island cells, Manhattan distance counts moves; subtract one to count the water cells between them.

methods.name: Mark islands, then use multi-source BFS
methods.idea: Expand from every cell of the first island until reaching the second.
steps: Find the two islands using a stack and four-directional neighbors.
Put every cell of the first island into a queue with water count 0.
Expand across water. Reaching the second island returns the number of water cells crossed.

methods.name: Two-pass distance DP
methods.idea: Compute each cell's Manhattan distance from the first island.
steps: Initialize cells of the first island to distance 0 and all other cells to infinity.
Scan top-left to bottom-right using upper and left neighbors, then reverse the scan using lower and right neighbors.
Take the minimum distance at a cell of the second island and subtract one to count water cells only.

methods.name: Compare all island-cell pairs
methods.idea: Find the closest pair of cells from the two islands.
steps: Collect the coordinates belonging to each island.
For every pair, compute abs(row1 - row2) + abs(col1 - col2) - 1.
Return the minimum. This is easy to follow but can take O(n⁴) time.

934.notation: n is the side length of the square grid. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

433.summary: Treat each valid gene as a node. One-character mutations are edges, so the answer is a shortest-path distance.
433.pitfall: The target must be in the bank. Return the number of mutations, not the number of genes on the path.

methods.name: BFS with generated neighbors
methods.idea: Generate valid next strings by changing one character at a time.
steps: Store allowed strings in a set for fast membership checks. The target must be allowed.
Start a queue at the initial string. For every position, try other alphabet characters and enqueue unseen valid strings.
BFS finds the fewest changes. Mutation returns changes; Word Ladder counts both endpoint words as well.

methods.name: Bidirectional BFS
methods.idea: Search from both endpoints and meet in the middle.
steps: Initialize one frontier at the start and another at the target, and track visited strings.
Expand the smaller frontier by generating valid one-character changes.
If a generated string is in the opposite frontier, the searches have met. Keep the problem's required distance convention.

methods.name: BFS by scanning the candidate list
methods.idea: Find neighbors by comparing the current string against every allowed string.
steps: Store the allowed strings and start a queue at the initial string.
Count differing positions for each candidate. Exactly one differing position makes it a neighbor.
Enqueue new neighbors and return when the target is reached. This avoids character generation but repeatedly scans the candidate list.

433.notation: N is the number of strings in bank, L is the string length, and A is the alphabet size (4). Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

127.summary: Treat each valid word as a node. One-letter transformations are edges, so use a shortest-path search.
127.pitfall: The target must be in wordList. Return the number of words, including the starting and ending words, not just the number of changes.

methods.name: BFS with generated neighbors
methods.idea: Generate valid next strings by changing one character at a time.
steps: Store allowed strings in a set for fast membership checks. The target must be allowed.
Start a queue at the initial string. For every position, try other alphabet characters and enqueue unseen valid strings.
BFS finds the fewest changes. Mutation returns changes; Word Ladder counts both endpoint words as well.

methods.name: Bidirectional BFS
methods.idea: Search from both endpoints and meet in the middle.
steps: Initialize one frontier at the start and another at the target, and track visited strings.
Expand the smaller frontier by generating valid one-character changes.
If a generated string is in the opposite frontier, the searches have met. Keep the problem's required distance convention.

methods.name: BFS by scanning the candidate list
methods.idea: Find neighbors by comparing the current string against every allowed string.
steps: Store the allowed strings and start a queue at the initial string.
Count differing positions for each candidate. Exactly one differing position makes it a neighbor.
Enqueue new neighbors and return when the target is reached. This avoids character generation but repeatedly scans the candidate list.

127.notation: N is the number of words in wordList, L is word length, and A is the alphabet size (26). Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

721.summary: Shared emails determine which accounts belong together. Collect and sort the unique emails in each connected group.
721.pitfall: Equal names do not imply the same person. Emails inside each returned account must be sorted and deduplicated.

methods.name: Union-Find over accounts
methods.idea: Accounts sharing an email belong to the same group.
steps: Map each email to an account index. When an email appears again, merge the two account indices.
After processing every account, collect unique emails under each group's representative.
Sort each group's emails and prepend the account name. Equal names alone do not justify a merge.

methods.name: DFS over emails
methods.idea: Treat emails as nodes and connect the emails within each account.
steps: Connect each account's first email with its other emails, and remember the owner name.
For each unvisited email, use a stack to collect its entire connected component.
Sort the component's unique emails and prepend the name. Repeat until every email is visited.

methods.name: BFS over emails
methods.idea: Use a queue to collect each connected email group.
steps: Build the same email graph and owner-name map.
For each unvisited email, start a queue and collect every reachable email.
Mark the component visited, sort its emails, and attach the owner's name.

721.notation: A is the number of accounts, T is the total number of email occurrences, and U is the number of distinct emails. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

990.summary: First use equalities to identify variables that must have the same value. Then check that inequalities do not contradict those groups.
990.pitfall: Do not decide inequalities before processing all equalities: later equalities may connect their variables indirectly.

methods.name: Union-Find
methods.idea: Merge all equal variables before testing inequalities.
steps: Create one group for each of the 26 letters.
For each equality, merge the two variables' groups.
For each inequality, compare the representatives. Equal representatives contradict the inequality, so return False.

methods.name: Connected components of equalities
methods.idea: Build a graph containing only equality relationships.
steps: Connect the two letters of each equality in both directions.
Traverse the graph to label each letter with its connected component.
Reject any inequality whose two letters have the same component label.

methods.name: Transitive closure
methods.idea: Explicitly compute every pair of variables forced to be equal.
steps: Start with self-equality and the given equality edges.
For each intermediate letter, mark pairs connected through that letter as reachable.
An inequality is impossible when its letters are reachable from each other. Otherwise all equations can be satisfied.

990.notation: Q is the number of equations and Σ is the alphabet size (26). Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1061.summary: Replace each character with the smallest character in its equivalence group. Choosing the smallest at each position minimizes the whole string.
1061.pitfall: A Union-Find representative is not automatically the smallest character. With union by size, separately record each group minimum.

methods.name: Union-Find with a group minimum
methods.idea: Replace every letter with the smallest letter in its equivalence group.
steps: Merge the pairs of letters from s1 and s2.
For each group representative, record the smallest member letter.
Look up each baseStr letter's group minimum and join the replacements into the answer.

methods.name: Character-graph search
methods.idea: Find all characters equivalent to each letter by graph traversal.
steps: Connect each paired character in both directions.
For each letter, traverse its connected component and record its smallest member.
Replace every character in baseStr with that recorded minimum.

methods.name: Set-based transitive closure
methods.idea: Grow each letter's set of equivalent characters.
steps: Start with each letter equivalent to itself and add the given pairs.
For each intermediate letter, expand any equivalence set containing it with its known equivalents.
Take the minimum character in each completed set and use it to transform baseStr.

1061.notation: P is the number of equivalent-character pairs, B is the length of baseStr, and Σ is the alphabet size (26). Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

839.summary: Connect directly similar words and count connected components. A similarity chain can connect words that are not directly similar.
839.pitfall: The zero-or-two-differences test relies on every word being an anagram of every other word. It is not sufficient for arbitrary strings.

methods.name: Pair comparison with Union-Find
methods.idea: Merge pairs that are identical or differ in exactly two positions.
steps: Compare every pair of words and count differing positions.
Since all words are anagrams, zero or two differences means the pair is similar. Merge those pairs.
Count distinct group representatives. Similarity chains belong to the same group.

methods.name: DFS on the similarity graph
methods.idea: Build a graph of directly similar words, then count connected components.
steps: Compare every pair and connect pairs differing in zero or two positions.
Start a stack search at each unvisited word and mark its component visited.
The number of fresh searches is the number of groups.

methods.name: BFS on the similarity graph
methods.idea: Collect connected word groups with a queue.
steps: Build the graph using the same pairwise similarity test.
For each unvisited word, run a queue-based traversal of its component.
Count one group for each new traversal.

839.notation: N is the number of strings and L is their common length. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

207.summary: Build edges from prerequisites to dependent courses. All courses can be completed exactly when this directed graph has no cycle.
207.pitfall: [a,b] means b → a. Independent courses also need to be included.

methods.name: Kahn's algorithm with a queue
methods.idea: Repeatedly take a course whose prerequisites are already complete.
steps: For each [course, prerequisite], add prerequisite → course. indegree counts unfinished prerequisites.
Enqueue all courses with indegree 0. Pop a course, append it to order, and decrease its next courses' indegrees.
Enqueue any course whose indegree becomes 0. If fewer than numCourses finish, there is a cycle. Return feasibility for 207, or the order for 210.

methods.name: DFS finishing order
methods.idea: Finish all dependent courses before adding the current course to the reverse order.
steps: Build prerequisite → course edges and track unvisited, active, and finished states.
Revisiting an active course detects a cycle. Reuse finished nodes instead of traversing them again.
Append each node after its neighbors finish, then reverse the result. Recursive depth can be large, so prefer the queue version for long chains.

methods.name: Topological sorting with a min-heap
methods.idea: Choose the smallest currently available course number.
steps: Build the graph and indegrees, then put zero-indegree courses into a min-heap.
Pop one course, append it to order, and reduce the indegrees of its dependents.
Push newly available courses. Check that all courses finish before returning True or the ordering.

207.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

210.summary: Build edges from prerequisites to dependent courses and return a topological order.
210.pitfall: [a,b] means b → a. Many valid orders may exist; your answer need not match the example exactly. Return [] for a cycle.

methods.name: Kahn's algorithm with a queue
methods.idea: Repeatedly take a course whose prerequisites are already complete.
steps: For each [course, prerequisite], add prerequisite → course. indegree counts unfinished prerequisites.
Enqueue all courses with indegree 0. Pop a course, append it to order, and decrease its next courses' indegrees.
Enqueue any course whose indegree becomes 0. If fewer than numCourses finish, there is a cycle. Return feasibility for 207, or the order for 210.

methods.name: DFS finishing order
methods.idea: Finish all dependent courses before adding the current course to the reverse order.
steps: Build prerequisite → course edges and track unvisited, active, and finished states.
Revisiting an active course detects a cycle. Reuse finished nodes instead of traversing them again.
Append each node after its neighbors finish, then reverse the result. Recursive depth can be large, so prefer the queue version for long chains.

methods.name: Topological sorting with a min-heap
methods.idea: Choose the smallest currently available course number.
steps: Build the graph and indegrees, then put zero-indegree courses into a min-heap.
Pop one course, append it to order, and reduce the indegrees of its dependents.
Push newly available courses. Check that all courses finish before returning True or the ordering.

210.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

269.summary: The first differing characters of adjacent words give ordering constraints. A topological order of those constraints is an alien alphabet.
269.pitfall: ["abc","ab"] is invalid even without a cycle. Include every observed letter and avoid double-counting duplicate edges.

methods.name: Extract constraints, then use Kahn's algorithm
methods.idea: Adjacent words reveal the required ordering of some letters.
steps: Include every observed character. For each adjacent word pair, add an edge for its first differing characters only.
Reject a longer word appearing before its own prefix. Avoid counting duplicate edges twice.
Topologically sort the character graph with a queue. A cycle means the dictionary is invalid.

methods.name: DFS on character constraints
methods.idea: Use DFS to order the letters after extracting dictionary constraints.
steps: Build the first-difference edges and check the prefix rule.
Use active and finished states to detect cycles and record finishing order.
Reverse the finishing order and translate node indices back to letters. Include letters with no constraints too.

methods.name: Min-heap topological sorting
methods.idea: Break ties between currently available letters with a min-heap.
steps: Build the same constraint graph, including isolated letters and the prefix check.
Push all zero-indegree letters. Repeatedly take the smallest available one.
Reduce its neighbors' indegrees and push newly available letters. If a cycle prevents completion, return an empty string.

269.notation: S is the sum of all word lengths, Σ is the number of observed characters, and E is the number of distinct ordering constraints. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1203.summary: Keep each group together while respecting item dependencies. Sort the group graph and item graph separately.
1203.pitfall: Give each ungrouped item a separate group. The group graph can contain a cycle even when the item graph does not.

methods.name: Two topological sorts with queues
methods.idea: Order the groups and items separately, then keep each group's items together.
steps: Give every ungrouped item its own new group. Build item edges and deduplicated cross-group edges.
Topologically sort both graphs with queues. A cycle in either graph makes the arrangement impossible.
Collect items by group in item-order, then concatenate those collections in group-order.

methods.name: Two topological sorts with DFS
methods.idea: Use DFS finishing order for both the group and item graphs.
steps: Assign separate groups to ungrouped items and build both dependency graphs.
Use DFS cycle detection and reverse finishing order to sort each graph. Deep chains may exceed the recursion limit.
Place items into group buckets according to item-order, then output buckets according to group-order.

methods.name: Two topological sorts with min-heaps
methods.idea: Use min-heaps to select available groups and items.
steps: Build separate item and group dependency graphs, giving each ungrouped item its own group.
Topologically sort both graphs using heaps and reject either graph if it contains a cycle.
Concatenate group buckets in group-order. Tie-breaking here does not guarantee a globally smallest final item sequence.

1203.notation: V is the number of items, G includes the new groups assigned to ungrouped items, and E counts dependency edges. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1857.summary: For a directed acyclic graph, track the maximum frequency of each color along a path. A cycle in any component requires -1.
1857.pitfall: Take a maximum for each color across alternative paths. Do not add counts from different paths together.

methods.name: Topological sorting with 26-color DP
methods.idea: Track the largest count of each color along paths reaching each node.
steps: Find a topological order. If not all nodes can be ordered, return -1 for a cycle.
At a node, add one to the count of its own color. Pass each color's maximum count to every next node.
Take the largest value in the DP table. Never add counts from separate paths together.

methods.name: One-color-at-a-time DP
methods.idea: Fix one color and solve a longest weighted path problem for that color.
steps: Compute a topological order once and reject cycles.
For each color present, give matching nodes weight 1 and all others weight 0. Propagate maximum totals in topological order.
Take the best total across colors. Reusing a one-dimensional DP array reduces memory.

methods.name: Memoized DFS
methods.idea: Store the best color-count vector for paths starting at each node.
steps: First reject cycles using a topological check.
Recursively obtain each child's vector and take the maximum separately for every color.
Add one for the current node's color, cache the vector, and take the global maximum. Long paths can exceed the recursion limit.

1857.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

787.summary: At most k stops means at most k + 1 flights. Keep track of the flight allowance as well as the price.
787.pitfall: A Bellman-Ford round must read only the previous array. Updating in place can accidentally use too many flights.

methods.name: Bounded Bellman-Ford
methods.idea: Increase the number of permitted flights one round at a time.
steps: Set the source price to 0 and other prices to infinity.
Repeat k + 1 rounds. Copy the previous prices and relax every flight using only the previous round's values.
Return the destination price, or -1 if it remains infinite. A stop limit of k allows at most k + 1 flights.

methods.name: Dijkstra with a flight-count state
methods.idea: Keep separate costs for reaching the same city with different numbers of flights.
steps: Build the flight adjacency list and start a heap with (0, src, 0).
Pop the cheapest state. Do not extend it once it has used k + 1 flights.
Update the cost for (next city, used flights + 1). Tracking only the city would lose valid alternatives.

methods.name: Memoized remaining-flight DP
methods.idea: Compute the cheapest remaining journey for a city and a flight allowance.
steps: Reaching the destination costs 0. Having no flights left elsewhere means failure.
Try every outgoing flight and add its price to the best result with one fewer flight allowed.
Cache results for each (city, allowance) pair. Return -1 if the source state has no valid route.

787.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1514.summary: Path probabilities multiply. Since edge probabilities are at most 1, extending a path cannot improve its probability.
1514.pitfall: An unreachable destination and a zero-probability route both return 0. The judge allows a small floating-point error.

methods.name: Maximum-probability Dijkstra
methods.idea: Process the most promising partial path first.
steps: Build the undirected probability graph. The start probability is 1.
Python has a min-heap, so store negative probabilities. Ignore outdated entries.
Multiply the current probability by each edge probability. Push improved results and return when the destination is finalized.

methods.name: Maximum-product Bellman-Ford
methods.idea: Repeatedly improve path probabilities by considering another edge.
steps: Start with probability 1 at the source and 0 elsewhere.
Copy the previous probability array and relax every undirected edge in both directions using multiplication.
Stop early if nothing changes, or after V - 1 rounds. Return the destination's probability.

methods.name: Array-based Dijkstra
methods.idea: Choose the best unprocessed node by scanning all nodes.
steps: Keep an array of best probabilities and a set of processed nodes.
Repeatedly select the unprocessed node with the highest probability.
Use its outgoing edges to improve neighbors. This avoids a heap but needs O(V²) selection work.

1514.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

505.summary: Treat positions where the ball stops as graph nodes. Rolling distance is the edge cost.
505.pitfall: Rolling through the destination is not enough: the ball must stop there. Different rolls can have different costs, so ordinary one-visit BFS is insufficient.

methods.name: Heap-based Dijkstra
methods.idea: Treat each stopping position as a node and rolling distance as the edge cost.
steps: moves rolls in each of four directions until a wall or boundary, returning the stopping cell and distance.
Pop the cheapest position from the heap. Ignore outdated entries and return when the destination is popped.
If a new route is shorter, update distance and push it. Passing through the destination without stopping does not count.
methods.code:
from typing import List
import heapq

class Solution:
    def shortestDistance(self, maze: List[List[int]], start: List[int], destination: List[int]) -> int:
        rows = len(maze)
        cols = len(maze[0])
        start = tuple(start)
        destination = tuple(destination)

        # Roll in one direction until reaching a wall or boundary.
        def moves(row, col):
            result = []
            for dr, dc in [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]:
                next_row, next_col = row, col
                steps = 0
                while (0 <= next_row + dr < rows and
                       0 <= next_col + dc < cols and
                       maze[next_row + dr][next_col + dc] == 0):
                    next_row += dr
                    next_col += dc
                    steps += 1
                if steps > 0:
                    result.append(((next_row, next_col), steps))
            return result

        distance = {start: 0}
        heap = [(0, start)]
        while heap:
            cost, position = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if cost != distance[position]:
                continue
            if position == destination:
                return cost

            for next_position, steps in moves(*position):
                new_cost = cost + steps
                if new_cost < distance.get(next_position, float("inf")):
                    distance[next_position] = new_cost
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (new_cost, next_position))

        return -1

methods.name: Array-based Dijkstra
methods.idea: Use a plain scan instead of a heap to find the nearest unfinished position.
steps: Generate rolling moves in all four directions.
Scan known, unvisited positions to choose the one with the smallest distance, then mark it visited.
Improve its neighbors' distances. Return on reaching the destination, or -1 when no position remains.

methods.name: Queue-based repeated relaxation
methods.idea: Revisit positions whenever a shorter route is discovered.
steps: Start a queue at the ball's position and store its distance as 0.
For every rolling move, compare the new distance with the best known distance.
If it improves, update the distance and queue that position again if necessary. Unlike ordinary BFS, a position may need processing more than once.

505.notation: V = R × C, where R and C are grid dimensions. L = max(R, C). Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

499.summary: Treat stopping positions as nodes, but stop a roll immediately when it reaches the hole. Compare both distance and instruction string.
499.pitfall: For equal distances, return the lexicographically smallest instruction string. A path with fewer instructions is not necessarily shorter or lexicographically smaller.

methods.name: Heap-based Dijkstra with path strings
methods.idea: Choose the smallest (distance, instruction string) pair.
steps: Generate rolling moves, stopping immediately if the ball reaches the hole.
Use (distance, path, position) in the heap. Ignore states worse than the stored best pair.
Update on a shorter distance or an equally short, lexicographically smaller path. Return the path when the hole is popped.

methods.name: Array-based Dijkstra with path strings
methods.idea: Scan unfinished positions to choose the best distance-and-path pair.
steps: Store the best (distance, path) pair for each reached position.
Choose the smallest pair among unfinished positions and roll in each direction.
Update better pairs and return the hole's path. Comparing path strings adds work beyond distance-only Dijkstra.

methods.name: Queue-based repeated relaxation
methods.time: Potentially exponential in the worst case due to repeated tie-breaking path improvements; not recommended for large inputs
methods.idea: Queue a position again whenever its distance or tie-breaking path improves.
steps: Start with distance 0 and an empty path at the ball.
Try every rolling move and compare the new (distance, path) pair with the stored pair.
Requeue improved positions. Equal-distance path improvements can be numerous; this method is for comparison, not large inputs.

499.notation: V = R × C, L = max(R, C), and P is the maximum instruction-string length. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1135.summary: Connect all cities at minimum total cost using a minimum spanning tree.
1135.pitfall: Match the one-based city labels to your arrays. Zero-cost and parallel connections are valid. Too few successful connections means the graph is disconnected.

methods.name: Kruskal with Union-Find
methods.idea: Pick the cheapest edges that connect different groups.
steps: Prepare the edges and sort them by cost. For water supply, include edges from virtual node 0 for wells.
Use find to compare endpoint groups. If they differ, merge them and add the edge cost.
A spanning tree needs V - 1 successful merges. If there are too few, the graph is disconnected.

methods.name: Prim with a min-heap
methods.idea: Grow one connected region using its cheapest outgoing connection.
steps: Build an undirected adjacency list and put the starting node into a heap at cost 0.
Pop an edge destination. If it is new, mark it visited and add its cost.
Push edges to unvisited neighbors. Check that all nodes have been reached before returning the total.

methods.name: Boruvka's algorithm
methods.idea: Each current group chooses its cheapest edge to another group.
steps: Scan all edges and record each group's cheapest outgoing edge.
Merge the selected edges with Union-Find, counting each successful merge once.
Repeat until one group remains. If no outgoing edge exists while groups remain separate, connection is impossible.

1135.notation: V is the number of nodes, E is the number of edges, n is the input size, and R/C are grid rows/columns. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1584.summary: Every pair of points has a possible edge with Manhattan-distance cost. Find a minimum spanning tree of this complete graph.
1584.pitfall: Use absolute coordinate differences, not Euclidean distance. Prim can avoid storing all O(n²) edges.

methods.name: Prim without storing all edges
methods.idea: Store only the cheapest known connection for each point.
steps: Set the first point's connection cost to 0 and all others to infinity.
Repeatedly select the unused point with the smallest connection cost and add that cost to the answer.
Compute its Manhattan distance to each unused point and lower their costs. This uses O(n) extra memory.

methods.name: Kruskal over all point pairs
methods.idea: Build and sort every possible connection.
steps: For every pair of points, calculate the Manhattan distance.
Sort these edges and use Union-Find to connect different groups.
Add costs for successful merges. This is straightforward but stores O(n²) edges.

methods.name: Boruvka over all point pairs
methods.idea: Let each connected component choose its cheapest connection outward.
steps: Build the complete list of pairwise Manhattan distances.
In each round, find the cheapest outgoing edge for every component.
Merge those edges with Union-Find and repeat until all points are connected.

1584.notation: n is the number of points; the complete graph has O(n²) edges. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1489.summary: Distinguish edges in every MST, some MSTs, or no MST. Return the original input indices.
1489.pitfall: Sorting edges must not lose their original indices. Do not also include a critical edge in the pseudo-critical list.

methods.name: Exclude or force each edge with Kruskal
methods.idea: Compare modified spanning-tree costs with the original minimum.
steps: Compute the baseline MST cost.
Exclude one edge and rebuild. If the graph disconnects or the cost rises, that edge is critical.
Otherwise force the edge into the tree and rebuild. If the cost stays at the baseline, the edge is pseudo-critical. Keep original input indices.

methods.name: Equal-weight groups and a contracted graph
methods.idea: Process equal-weight edges together using the components formed by cheaper edges.
steps: For each weight, map endpoints to their current Union-Find representatives and keep edges between different groups.
Temporarily remove each candidate edge from the contracted graph. If its endpoints become disconnected, it is critical; otherwise it is pseudo-critical.
Only after classifying the whole weight group should its components be merged. Distinguish parallel edges by their original indices.

methods.name: Enumerate spanning trees (small inputs only)
methods.idea: List all spanning trees to make the definitions explicit.
steps: Try each combination of V - 1 edges and use Union-Find to reject cycles.
Keep only trees with the smallest total cost.
Edges in every minimum tree are critical. Edges in some but not all are pseudo-critical. Combinatorial growth makes this unsuitable for large inputs.

1489.notation: C(E,V-1) counts candidate edge combinations. T in the space bound is the number of minimum spanning trees retained during enumeration. Space means extra memory, excluding the input. α is the inverse Ackermann function used in Union-Find bounds; it grows extremely slowly.

1168.summary: Represent a well as an edge from virtual node 0 to its house, then find a minimum spanning tree including that virtual node.
1168.pitfall: Include the virtual node when sizing arrays. Parallel pipes and zero costs are valid; choose only connections needed to supply all houses.

steps: Prepare the edges and sort them by cost. For water supply, include edges from virtual node 0 for wells.

A spanning tree needs V - 1 successful merges. If there are too few, the graph is disconnected.

methods.idea: Grow one connected region using its cheapest outgoing connection.
steps: Build an undirected adjacency list and put the starting node into a heap at cost 0.
Pop an edge destination. If it is new, mark it visited and add its cost.
Push edges to unvisited neighbors. Check that all nodes have been reached before returning the total.
